steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting HateModerate, a dataset for testing whether hate speech detectors follow platforms' content moderation policies. Explain the motivation, how the dataset was built, and what we found when testing existing detectors and fine-tuning on it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Hate speech on social media and existing detection work / moderation tools
- Open question: do detectors conform to platforms' content policies?
- HateModerate dataset and choice of Facebook's guidelines
- Construction process
- Evaluation of detectors and improvements from fine-tuning

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - Facebook, Reddit, Twitter/X: information exchange but also undesirable content (hateful speech, misinformation, graphic violence, pornography)
  - NLP approaches, resources, open-source tools for hate speech detection
  - platforms' content moderation tools; Facebook's automatic moderator detected 95% unwanted content before seen by a user
- Open question
  - do detectors' behaviors conform to content policies?
  - content policies = platform rules on what it moderates
  - Facebook: 41 community standards guidelines for hate speech as of Nov 2022; Figure 1 shows 3 examples
  - policies = "contract" between users and platform; otherwise moderation surprising, hurts transparency/accountability
  - trust issues -> Reddit blackouts, users cannot access content normally
  - existing datasets can't answer it: unique platform rules, e.g. Facebook moderates ads on homosexual therapies
  - custom rules underrepresented -> underestimate model failures
- HateModerate
  - 7.6k hateful and non-hateful examples, 41 Facebook guidelines
  - among published moderation rules, chose Facebook's: most comprehensive of all platforms, good clarity
- Construction (six steps, Figure 2)
  - 28 graduate students as annotators; some search existing datasets for hateful examples per policy
  - augment guidelines with few matches via GPT engine
  - 16 more annotators verify each hateful example
  - retrieve difficult non-hateful examples closely resembling hateful ones
  - GPT-generated non-hateful examples
  - 4 more annotators verify non-hateful examples
  - Krippendorf's alpha: 0.521 hateful, 0.809 non-hateful
- Evaluation
  - Google's Perspective API, OpenAI's Moderation API, Facebook's RoBERTa, Cardiff NLP's RoBERTa
  - severe policies (violence) prioritized over less severe (stereotyping)
  - OpenAI conforms best
  - others: high failure rates on non-hateful examples
  - add HateModerate to training data of top-downloaded HuggingFace model -> better on HateModerate and HateCheck, original test set comparable
  - fine-tuning comparison with DynaHate: HateModerate better than existing datasets
  - importance for model conformity to policies

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Social media platforms like Facebook, Reddit, and Twitter/X have made it easier for users to exchange information, but they also expose users to undesirable content, including hateful speech, misinformation, graphic violence, and pornography. To protect users from the massive amount of hateful content, existing work has been actively investigating new NLP approaches for hate speech detection and providing new resources and open-source tools for studying it. At the same time platforms also invested in building content moderation tools and had great success with them, e.g., Facebook's automatic content moderator detected 95% of unwanted content before it is seen by a user.

Even with this existing work on hate speech, there is an important question that is not well addressed: Do the behaviors of hate speech detectors conform to the content policies of platforms? Content policies are rules specified by a platform about what content it moderates. For example, as of Nov 2022, Facebook specifies 41 community standards guidelines for moderating hate speech; Figure 1 shows 3 examples of Facebook's guidelines. The content policies are like a "contract" between users and the platform. If the automated content moderators do not conform to the policies, their decisions may be surprising to users, and this undermines the transparency and accountability of the moderation system. These trustworthiness issues have led to incidents such as Reddit blackouts, which prevent users from accessing the contents normally. Also, this question cannot be answered directly with existing hate speech datasets, because many platforms have unique moderation rules, e.g., Facebook moderates advertisements on homosexual therapies. Our investigation shows that these custom rules are not well represented in the existing hate speech datasets, and this causes the models' failures in conforming to these rules to be underestimated.

To assess whether automated content moderators conform to content policies, in this paper we propose a dataset called HateModerate. It consists of 7.6k hateful and non-hateful examples for the 41 community standards guidelines on Facebook. Among the moderation rules published in existing work, we chose Facebook's community standards guidelines for hate speech, since previous work shows it is the most comprehensive among all platforms and it also has good clarity.

- construction, six steps (Figure 2): 28 graduate students as annotators, some search existing datasets for hateful examples per policy; GPT engine generates hateful examples for guidelines with too few; 16 more annotators verify hateful examples; retrieve difficult non-hateful examples resembling hateful ones; GPT-generated non-hateful examples; 4 more annotators verify non-hateful
- agreement (Krippendorf's alpha): 0.521 / 0.809
- evaluate Google's Perspective API, OpenAI's Moderation API, Facebook's RoBERTa, Cardiff NLP's RoBERTa
- findings: severe policies (violence) prioritized over less severe (stereotyping); OpenAI conforms best; others high failure rates on non-hateful
- adding HateModerate to training of top-downloaded HuggingFace model -> better on HateModerate and HateCheck, original test set comparable
- fine-tuning vs DynaHate: HateModerate better

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Social media platforms like Facebook, Reddit, and Twitter/X have made it easier for users to exchange information, but they also expose users to undesirable content, including hateful speech, misinformation, graphic violence, and pornography. To protect users from the massive amount of hateful content, existing work has been actively investigating new NLP approaches for hate speech detection and providing new resources and open-source tools for studying it. At the same time platforms also invested in building content moderation tools and had great success with them, e.g., Facebook's automatic content moderator detected 95% of unwanted content before it is seen by a user.

Even with this existing work on hate speech, there is an important question that is not well addressed: Do the behaviors of hate speech detectors conform to the content policies of platforms? Content policies are rules specified by a platform about what content it moderates. For example, as of Nov 2022, Facebook specifies 41 community standards guidelines for moderating hate speech; Figure 1 shows 3 examples of Facebook's guidelines. The content policies are like a "contract" between users and the platform. If the automated content moderators do not conform to the policies, their decisions may be surprising to users, and this undermines the transparency and accountability of the moderation system. These trustworthiness issues have led to incidents such as Reddit blackouts, which prevent users from accessing the contents normally. Also, this question cannot be answered directly with existing hate speech datasets, because many platforms have unique moderation rules, e.g., Facebook moderates advertisements on homosexual therapies. Our investigation shows that these custom rules are not well represented in the existing hate speech datasets, and this causes the models' failures in conforming to these rules to be underestimated.

To assess whether automated content moderators conform to content policies, in this paper we propose a dataset called HateModerate. It consists of 7.6k hateful and non-hateful examples for the 41 community standards guidelines on Facebook. Among the moderation rules published in existing work, we chose Facebook's community standards guidelines for hate speech, since previous work shows it is the most comprehensive among all platforms and it also has good clarity.

We construct HateModerate using a six-step process, which is illustrated in Figure 2. First, we recruit a group of 28 graduate students as the annotators. Some of these students manually search existing datasets for hateful examples that match each policy. Second, some guidelines have too few matched examples, so we augment these guidelines by generating hateful examples with the GPT engine. Third, 16 additional annotators manually verify each hateful example to make sure that the searched and generated examples really match the criteria. Fourth, once the hateful examples are collected, for each guideline we retrieve difficult non-hateful examples from existing datasets which closely resemble the hateful examples, to help detect the model failures. Fifth, in a similar way we augment guidelines with non-hateful examples generated by GPT. Sixth, 4 additional annotators manually verify each non-hateful example. The average agreement rate (Krippendorf's alpha) on the match/unmatch of the hateful and non-hateful examples is 0.521 and 0.809.

After we construct HateModerate, we use it to examine state-of-the-art hate speech detectors against each policy. The models we examine are Google's Perspective API, OpenAI's Moderation API, Facebook's RoBERTa model and Cardiff NLP's RoBERTa model. We observe the following things. First, all models prioritize more severe policies (e.g., violence) over less severe policies (e.g., stereotyping). Second, the OpenAI model conforms the best to the content policies. Third, other than OpenAI, the models generally have high failure rates on non-hateful examples. After seeing these model failures we also look at how to improve the models' conformity to policies. When we add HateModerate to the training dataset of a top-downloaded model on HuggingFace, the model's performance on HateModerate and HateCheck is significantly improved, while the performance on the original test set stays comparable. We also do a fine-tuning experiment comparing HateModerate and DynaHate, and it shows that HateModerate outperforms existing datasets. These results show the importance of our dataset for improving the model conformity to content policies.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Social media platforms such as Facebook, Reddit, and Twitter/X have helped users exchange information, but they also expose users to undesirable content, including hateful speech, misinformation, graphic violence, and pornography. To protect users from a massive amount of hateful content, existing work has been vigorously investigating new NLP approaches and providing new resources and open-source tools for studying hate speech detection [2,3,4,5,6,7]. Meanwhile, platforms have also invested in and achieved great success in building content moderation tools [8,9], e.g., Facebook's automatic content moderator detected 95% of unwanted content before it is seen by a user [8].

Despite the existing work on hate speech, an important question remains not well addressed: Do hate speech detectors' behaviors conform to platforms' content policies? Content policies are platform-specified rules on what content it moderates. For example, as of Nov 2022, Facebook specifies 41 community standards guidelines for moderating hate speech [1]; Figure 1 shows 3 examples of Facebook's guidelines. The content policies serve as a "contract" between users and the platform; if automated content moderators do not conform to the policies, their decisions may be surprising to users, undermining the transparency and accountability of the moderation system. Such trustworthiness issues have led to incidents such as Reddit blackouts, which prevent users from accessing the contents normally [10]. Meanwhile, this question cannot be directly answered using existing hate speech datasets, because many platforms have unique moderation rules, e.g., Facebook moderates advertisements on homosexual therapies. Our investigation shows that these custom rules are not well represented in existing hate speech datasets, which causes the models' failures in conforming to these rules to be underestimated.

To assess the conformity of automated content moderators to content policies, this paper proposes a dataset called HateModerate, which consists of 7.6k hateful and non-hateful examples for the 41 community standards guidelines on Facebook. Among the moderation rules published in existing work [11,1,12], we choose Facebook's community standards guidelines for hate speech [1], as previous work shows it is the most comprehensive among all platforms [13] and it has good clarity.

HateModerate is constructed using the six-step process illustrated in Figure 2. First, we recruit a group of 28 graduate students as the annotators, some of whom manually search existing datasets for hateful examples matching each policy. Second, since some guidelines contain too few matched examples, we augment these guidelines by generating hateful examples with the GPT engine. Third, to ensure that the searched and generated examples indeed match the criteria, 16 additional annotators manually verify each hateful example. Fourth, after the hateful examples are collected, for each guideline we retrieve difficult non-hateful examples from existing datasets that closely resemble the hateful examples, to help detect model failures. Fifth, we similarly augment guidelines with GPT-generated non-hateful examples. Sixth, 4 additional annotators manually verify each non-hateful example. The average agreement rates (Krippendorf's alpha) on the match/unmatch of hateful and non-hateful examples are 0.521 and 0.809.

After constructing HateModerate, we use the dataset to examine state-of-the-art hate speech detectors against each policy. Specifically, we examine Google's Perspective API [14], OpenAI's Moderation API [15], Facebook's RoBERTa model [16] and Cardiff NLP's RoBERTa model [7]. We make the following observations. First, all models prioritize more severe policies (e.g., violence) over less severe policies (e.g., stereotyping); second, the OpenAI model conforms best to the content policies; third, apart from OpenAI, models generally have high failure rates on non-hateful examples. Having observed these failures, we further investigate how to improve the models' conformity to policies. By adding HateModerate to the training dataset of a top-downloaded model on HuggingFace, the model's performance on HateModerate and HateCheck [12] is significantly improved while its performance on the original test set remains comparable. We also conduct a fine-tuning experiment comparing HateModerate and DynaHate, which shows that HateModerate outperforms existing datasets. These results highlight the importance of our dataset for improving model conformity to content policies.
